articles.title: Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv, damages major bridge
articles.summary: Russian forces hammered energy ​infrastructure around Ukraine’s capital with missiles and drones overnight, straining Kyiv’s power supply ‌and heating systems as temperatures headed towards zero, officials said on Saturday.
articles.body: Russian forces hammered energy ​infrastructure around Ukraine’s capital with missiles and drones overnight, straining Kyiv’s power supply ‌and heating systems as temperatures headed towards zero, officials said on Saturday. Explosions rocked the city as Russia fired multiple waves of ballistic missiles, several of which hit and damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Strikes ​on energy facilities outside Kyiv — including systems sending power from two nuclear plants to ​the city and Ukraine’s central regions — caused serious damage, the energy ministry ⁠said. “The capital is facing serious difficulties with its electricity, water, and heat supplies,” President Volodymyr ​Zelenskyy said on X, adding that substations in five other regions were also hit. He said Russia ​had launched 36 ballistic missiles, only four of which were intercepted, according to Ukraine’s air force. It added that air defenses had downed 149 out of 172 drones. At least two ​people were killed and around a dozen others wounded across Ukraine in the overnight attacks, ​which also damaged homes, businesses and non-residential buildings, authorities said. Moscow’s defense ministry said it carried out a massive ‌strike ⁠on what it described as targets in Ukraine’s military-industrial sector, as well as energy and transport infrastructure in and around Kyiv. Russia has stepped up air attacks on Ukraine as its ground offensive has largely stalled, pounding energy infrastructure in major cities with difficult-to-intercept missiles and drones more than ​4-1/2 years into its ​full-scale invasion. It has expanded ⁠its campaign in recent weeks to target Kyiv’s bridges, snarling traffic in the city of more than 3 million people. Saturday’s strikes come days before ​a new round of three-way talks in Abu Dhabi between Ukrainian and ​Russian officials, ⁠as part of a US-backed peace push that has so far yielded few results. “Russia is preparing for trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said on X. The attacks also ⁠follow ​recent US midterm elections that have raised hopes in Ukraine for ​stronger support against Russia’s war from a Democratic-controlled Congress. “We are counting on the US Congress to give more attention ​to Ukraine, because Russia keeps increasing the number of its attacks,” Zelenskyy added.

articles.title: ‘Patiala Peg’, ‘5 Tara Theke’ among 4 Diljit Dosanjh songs barred from Indore concert
articles.summary: INDORE: Four songs by Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh have been barred from his November 15 concert in Indore over concerns that their alleged promotion of
articles.body: INDORE: Four songs by Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh have been barred from his November 15 concert in Indore over concerns that their alleged promotion of alcohol and violence could adversely affect children and others, officials said on Saturday.The songs are "Patiala Peg", "5 Tara Theke", "Jeb Vicho Feem", and "Jatt Fire Karda", they said.The district child protection officer issued directions to this effect to the manager of the concert venue following a complaint by Chandigarh-based Dr Punditrao Dharenavar, officials added.The letter sent to the venue manager stated that children above the age of five would be allowed to attend the live concert and that the songs could have an adverse impact on them.It also referred to a July 22, 2019, order of the Punjab and Haryana high court, which directed the police in Punjab, Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh to ensure that songs glorifying liquor, wine, drugs and violence were not played, including at live performances.The court had highlighted the impact of such songs on young children.In his complaint, Dharenavar referred to the high court order and urged the authorities to prohibit Dosanjh from performing the four songs, even if their lyrics were altered.He also sought a ban on the singer inviting children on stage during the concert and wearing two crossed silver bullet belts, also known as bandoliers, or dummy metallic silver cartridges on his chest during the live show.(With inputs from PTI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Indore | Silver Rate in Indore | Bank Holidays in Indore | Public Holidays in Indore | Petrol Price in Indore | Diesel Price in Indore | CNG Price in Indore | LPG Price in IndoreStay updated with the latest Indore news. articles.title: ‘They started bombing us with drones’: Russian attacks unnerve Zaporizhzhia
articles.summary: A region once offering refuge becomes increasingly dangerous, as 50 people are killed in a single attack.
articles.body:
Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine – There are only eight people left in Volodymyr’s village. That was the last count he remembers before deciding to leave.

“We were in the cellar when they started bombing us with drones,” he said, nervously rubbing his red, blistered hands together. “As you can see, I was completely burned.”

Last week, he fled his home in Preobrazhenka, just over 40km (25 miles) from where he now sits in a shelter for displaced people in the regional capital, Zaporizhzhia.

The villages south of Zaporizhzhia have been coming under escalating Russian attacks.

On November 2, in one of this year’s deadliest attacks in Ukraine, nine Russian glide bombs struck the town of Komyshuvakha , killing at least 50 people. Many had gathered to receive humanitarian aid at a local school. Several people are still missing, feared dead under the rubble.

The constant threat of bombs and drones makes everyday life almost unbearable.

Over the past three years, this war has proven that an army no longer needs boots on the ground.

The arrival of Russian First-Person-View (FPV) drones overhead is often a sign of the Russian infantry’s gradual advance. Well-documented footage shows these drones deliberately targeting vehicles and civilians on the streets. Ukrainians say drones have stalked civilians in cities including Kherson , Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

Now, Zaporizhzhia is showing some of the same warning signs.

The city administration is doing what it can to protect residents, installing anti-drone netting over streets and civilian infrastructure in the Cosmos neighbourhood. But boarded-up windows and bombed-out buildings across the city show how difficult it is to mitigate the threat once the drones arrive.

Denys Knysh, a regional military administration official, says authorities are preparing to relocate the shelter where Volodymyr is staying to another neighbourhood “if the situation gets worse”.

Many in the shelter are elderly or have limited mobility. Some lack the documents they need to relocate, making evacuation more difficult.

Others prefer to stay in Zaporizhzhia, close to their former homes, holding on to hope that the war will end and they can return.

Since the beginning of the war, Zaporizhzhia has provided refuge for thousands of internally displaced people fleeing Russia’s occupation. People have arrived from cities like Mariupol and Melitopol, which fell under Russian control early in the conflict.

Now, as the security situation deteriorates, some of those who once fled to Zaporizhzhia for safety face the prospect of having to leave again.

Alina, who works in a flower shop beneath protective drone netting, said, “Of course I may have to leave, but I don’t want to.”

She hears the buzz of Russian drones almost every day.

Nearby, along the Pryberezhna Highway that follows the river, every petrol station and business is covered in the protective netting.

“It’s scary and dangerous, everything is flying around. Just today a drone flew over us,” said Nataliia, an employee at a petrol station.

Earlier that day, Russian Banderol missiles, a type of low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile, struck a shopping mall and the main bridge into the city. An FPV drone also hit a city bus.

Zaporizhzhia still has signs of normality. Twinkling lights hang over restaurant terraces and some streets still buzz with life.

People gradually adapt to each new threat. It starts with streets covered in nets. Then drone jammers on the roofs of city buses. Bridges bear gaping holes from attacks. Children walk around carrying drone detectors.

Knysh says authorities are ready to evacuate the city if and when that time comes.

“It’s very difficult to calculate [how many people are left in the city] because every day people leave Zaporizhzhia,” he told Al Jazeera. “The demographic in Google doesn’t correspond to the reality.”

articles.title: When a 1,000-meal catering order was cancelled in 2020, a New York founder gave the food to hospital workers; six years later, her business says it has donated 4 million meals
articles.summary: A cancelled catering order became the starting point for a food business with a much larger purpose.
articles.body: A cancelled catering order became the starting point for a food business with a much larger purpose. When the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted operations in New York City in 2020, The Migrant Kitchen, a newly launched catering company, was left with 1,000 prepared meals after an order was cancelled. Instead of letting the food go to waste, the team decided to donate it to hospital workers treating patients during the health crisis. What began as an unexpected response to a difficult situation eventually developed into a wider effort to address food insecurity while creating employment opportunities.The story was highlighted in a February 24, 2026, profile published by Syracuse University Today and subsequently featured by the university's Shaw Center on March 2, 2026. The university reported that the immigrant-led food enterprise had donated 4 million meals while building opportunities for a workforce made up largely of immigrants. The initiative also reflects Tanney's belief that food can provide more than nourishment, offering dignity, support and a sense of community to people facing difficult circumstances.From an emergency response to a larger food operationThe initial donation quickly attracted more requests for meals. Tanney recalled that the business went from serving 1,000 meals to receiving continuous calls for help. To respond, she and The Migrant Kitchen's founder, Daniel Dorado, reached out to restaurant industry contacts, many of whom had lost work because of the pandemic. They invited them to join the effort and prepare food for people who needed it.The growing demand encouraged Tanney and Dorado to turn the emergency response into a structured operation. They brought together restaurants, government agencies and community organisations to prepare and distribute thousands of meals every day. This approach allowed the initiative to expand beyond its original catering business and develop into a social enterprise focused on addressing food insecurity.In 2020, the two established JD Enterprises, a social impact food company. Tanney now serves as president of JD Meals, which operates as part of the organisation. Through its nonprofit arm, The Migrant Kitchen Initiative, the enterprise has donated 4 million meals to people in need, according to Syracuse University.Supporting communities facing food insecurityThe organisation's work now extends to people living in temporary housing and those relying on emergency assistance. Tanney said the team serves thousands of meals daily to residents in New York City's shelter system and at emergency sites. The initiative also focuses on making sure the food reflects the cultural backgrounds and preferences of the communities receiving it. Tanney works with kitchen staff, government representatives, community leaders and other stakeholders to understand local needs and coordinate resources. This helps the organisation provide meals that are not only accessible but also familiar and culturally appropriate.Another important part of its approach is its workforce. The company employs roughly 100 people, many of whom are immigrants. Tanney has described this as a continuation of The Migrant Kitchen's founding mission. She believes having employees who share experiences with the communities receiving the meals helps the organisation understand their circumstances and serve them with greater empathy.The business has also expanded its work beyond New York. In autumn 2025, JD Meals entered Philadelphia after city leaders approached Tanney's team for help strengthening emergency meal distribution for residents experiencing housing instability. The expansion became part of a broader effort to support recovery, stability and dignity among vulnerable residents.How education shaped the initiativeTanney's interest in community service began well before the pandemic. She volunteered with food pantries as a teenager and wanted to pursue a career that would allow her to create positive change. However, she had not initially decided how she would put that ambition into practice. Her studies at Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs helped her develop the skills needed to work across different sectors. She graduated with a bachelor's degree in policy studies in 2005 and later pursued a master's degree in public administration at Baruch College in New York City.At Syracuse, she worked under Professor Bill Coplin, who founded the policy studies programme. His emphasis on practical problem-solving, collaboration and community engagement influenced her approach to social impact work. Her experience also included volunteering with the Syracuse University Literacy Corps, interning with the affordable housing nonprofit Home HeadQuarters and participating in a programme that placed students in New York City schools after the September 11 attacks.Coplin later praised Tanney's ability to bring people together and address community needs through practical solutions. He said her work reflected the values of collaboration and hands-on problem-solving that the programme sought to develop. Tanney's work has also received professional recognition. She was included in Crain's New York Business magazine's 40 Under 40 list and named among The Spruce Eats' Women Culinarians You Should Know. She also received the Organisational Hero Award from the New York City chapter of the Association of Fundraising Professionals.What began with an unexpected cancellation has therefore grown into an organised effort involving restaurants, public agencies, community partners and an immigrant workforce. For Tanney, the experience demonstrates how individuals and businesses can respond to an immediate crisis while building something that continues to support communities long after the emergency has passed.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Radical’ or ‘hero’?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon
articles.summary: The hard-left leader has transformed into a real contender in next year presidential elections.
articles.body:
Hard-left French leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has been described as a “radical” by right-wing opponents, a “despot” by former allies and a “hero” by some of the students who have taken to the streets in nationwide protests .

The leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party has emerged as the strongest contender on the left and potential challenger to far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential election.

On Saturday, Melenchon is presenting his programme at a rally in Le Bourget, north of Paris, a day after it was published online.

Among his proposals, he wants to lower the retirement age to 60 and raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro ($1,900) a month; pull France out of NATO and renationalise parts of the economy.

He wants the European Central Bank to stop France repaying the debt it holds, effectively transforming the debt instead to a permanent interest-free loan – a move he hopes would give the government more room to spend.

On Europe, he envisions France remaining in the EU, but he wants to refuse rules that conflict with the nation’s social, environmental or economic programmes, setting up a potentially confrontational relationship with Brussels.

‘He is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations’

His party is gaining momentum as protests led by students in mid-September swelled to include several groups angry about failing public services, rising living costs and uncertain futures.

The hard-left leader has been hailed at marches, some of which have seen vandalism and looting.

“His strength is that he is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations: better wages, money in education, a lot of welfare measures, no austerity cuts which appease people who are fed up with the cost of living,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute. “He is the vote of the protesters.”

But some say his policies are radical and unrealistic.

France’s finances and borrowing are under scrutiny as its budget deficit and debt levels are high, raising further doubts on how Melenchon’s ambitious spending plans, particularly on social programmes and public investment, could be implemented.

Some economists warn that his plans could cause investors to sell French government bonds, making it more expensive for France to borrow and potentially causing losses.

“Borrowing money and deciding not to give it back – that’s called theft,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in September, regarding such proposals.

LFI says higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations – another pillar of Melenchon’s campaign – would finance its spending plans.

His proposals include a minimum 2 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires, restoring France’s wealth tax and increasing taxes on large inheritances.

“Financial capital has benefitted, and it is the one that should pay,” he said in October.

His programme draws on a tradition of left-wing economic interventionism, rooted partly in Keynesian thought, that argues that the state should play an active role in the economy to reduce inequalities generated by the market.

“Because this tradition of state intervention in economic and social affairs has been abandoned by most other political parties, the fact that LFI continues to define itself through such interventionism creates an impression of radicalism,” said political analyst Beligh Nabli, a professor of public law at UPEC-Paris XII. “Yet, this radicalism is only relative – it appears radical when compared to other contemporary political offerings, but from the perspective of the history of social democracy, it is not radical at all.”

Melenchon, 75, was born in Morocco to French parents.

He moved to France as a child where he later graduated in philosophy and modern literature. In the 1980s, he joined the Socialist Party, but distanced himself from it when it shifted towards more liberal economics.

In 2008, he finally quit the Socialists and founded the Left Party, which would later evolve into LFI. The party appealed to working-class voters and marginalised communities and became popular with young people.

According to this week’s polls, the presidential candidate is polling between 17.5 to 18 percent, widening the gap with his rivals in the left camp.

Trailing behind is Raphael Glucksmann, who leads the centre-left Place Publique party and secured the backing of the Socialist Party after winning a joint primary in October. Further back, and running on their own ticket – the Communist Party’s Fabien Roussel, Marine Tondelier’s Greens party and independent Francois Ruffin.

The left-wing bloc is undecided on the LFI.

As Melenchon holds a significant lead, smaller parties are weighing whether to support him to give a left-wing alliance a better shot.

Glucksmann has ruled that out, but others are pondering the situation.

“This will be one of the key debates throughout the presidential campaign,” said Nabil.

Another source of tension across the French left is Melenchon’s strong support of Palestine.

He has repeatedly refused to describe Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a term other left-wing politicians, including Glucksmann, have been reluctant to use.

Melenchon has also faced accusations from political opponents on the left that his rhetoric fuels anti-Semitism, claims he rejects.

But Melenchon’s popularity is nowhere close to that of National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen.

The far-right leader, who challenged President Emmanuel Macron in a second round in the past two elections, would easily win in a run-off against Melenchon, leading 70 percent to 30 percent, according to a Toluna Harris Interactive poll conducted in October.

Analysts say his economic programme is not the only obstacle. His combative political style and reputation for confrontation over compromise hinder his chances of broadening support beyond a core base.

“In France, it is often said that to win a presidential election, one must campaign from the centre. Yet, the defining characteristic of the LFI programme is that it is not centrist – that is precisely what makes it disruptive. He seeks victory, but not a victory from the centre,” Nabli said.

His leadership has also been criticised.

Several former allies have said their break with the party was driven by both Melenchon’s management style and political disagreements.

Former LFI candidate Thomas Guenole has described the movement as a “dictatorship” governed by “an autocrat”, while former lawmaker Raquel Garrido said there was a left that agreed with LFI’s programme but not with the party leader’s “methods”.

Former close ally Clementine Autain has likewise accused LFI of becoming “authoritarian”.

“He is the ‘supreme leader’,” said Reland at the Global Policy Institute. “The party is very organised, but it’s not a democratic party at all.”

articles.title: 11-night Caribbean cruise abruptly canceled after Coast Guard detains ship
articles.summary: After the U.S. Coast Guard identified significant deficiencies, the MSC Poesia was detained in Miami, stranding over 2,000 cruise passengers. An attorney weighed in.
articles.body: A major cruise line abruptly canceled an 11-night voyage to the Caribbean this week when the U.S. Coast Guard detained its ship in Miami. The Coast Guard announced on Nov. 3 that MSC Poesia had been detained due to deficiencies with systems aboard the ship. "The Coast Guard cannot currently comment on the specifics of an ongoing Port State Control Examination, but we have identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel that we are addressing with MSC," said Capt. Frank Florio, commander, U.S. Coast Guard Sector Miami, in a press release issued by the Coast Guard. OUTRAGED CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST COMPANY'S 'IDIOTIC' NEW DRESS CODE CRACKDOWN The MSC Poesia will remain detained at the Miami port until the deficiencies are fixed and the ship is cleared to depart, the release added. "We have made the difficult decision to cancel the current sailing," an MSC Cruises spokesperson told Fox News Digital about the situation. "We recognize how disappointing and frustrating this news is for our guests, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption to their holiday." "Prior to departure, a regulatory matter arose that required resolution. articles.title: Iraq’s FM says external parties using Iraqi soil to attack neighbours
articles.summary: Iraqi foreign minister tells Al Jazeera that Baghdad is investigating attacks on the Gulf launched from its territory.
articles.body:
Iraq has evidence that external parties have been using its territory to launch attacks on neighbouring countries, its foreign minister told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview on Saturday.

Baghdad is investigating attacks launched from Iraqi territory against Gulf states and is seeking to resolve disagreements with Saudi Arabia through dialogue, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said.

Saudi Arabia has accused Iran-aligned groups operating in Iraq of attacking its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that drone attacks on the kingdom’s East-West pipeline originated from Iraqi territory.

Hussein told Al Jazeera that Baghdad was negotiating with Iran-aligned armed factions to bring their weapons under state control and the process must be pursued through dialogue rather than force.

He also said Iraq was in contact with Tehran regarding the issue of weapons held by Iraqi factions.

Iraq’s government had initially established a deadline for armed factions to bring their weapons under state control by September 30, when the US-led international coalition to combat ISIL (ISIS) was set to end their mandate and leave the country.

However, it pushed back the deadline to June 2027 after encountering resistance to the policy, despite long-standing pressure from the US to fulfil its disarmament pledge.

On Iraq’s balancing act between Tehran and Washington, Hussein confirmed that the US had formally requested the closure of all but two border crossings with Iran.

He added that while Iraq welcomed friendship and an alliance with Tehran, it rejected interference in its internal affairs.

The foreign minister also said that Iraq had lost about $60bn from the suspension of oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, but that shipments have resumed after understandings were reached with Washington and Tehran.

On the issue of combatting ISIL after the coalition pullout, Hussein said that Iraq, Syria, Jordan and Turkiye have formed a committee to fight the group’s presence in Syria.

For Al Jazeera’s full interview with the Iraqi FM, tune in at 21:00 Doha time (18:00 GMT) on Sunday.

articles.title: Why can't Congress break free from Gandhi family? Sonia responds to nepotism charge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi appeared to sidestep questions about the Gandhi family's continued control of the party and allegations of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi appeared to sidestep questions about the Gandhi family's continued control of the party and allegations of nepotism during an interview with British newspaper The Guardian, saying the question of its leadership should be put to the party itself.“You would have to ask the party,” she told the interviewer when asked why the Congress had not moved beyond the Gandhi family's leadership.The newspaper said Sonia Gandhi “skates over the question of nepotism”, quoting her response to the charge that the party is controlled by one family. “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have,” Sonia Gandhi said in a vague answer to nepotism charge.The interview was published on Saturday, alongside an edited extract from her memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love", which is due to be released early next week.Gandhi grip amid Congress lossesSonia maintained that the Congress could still emerge as a credible alternative to the BJP. However, the interviewer noted that many people remained unconvinced after the party's repeated electoral defeats.The article pointed to the Congress's decline under Rahul Gandhi's leadership. After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The party is now in power in only a few states, while the BJP's Hindutva ideology has become the country's dominant political force.The newspaper observed that the Gandhi family's continued control had made it difficult for the Congress to shake off allegations of nepotism and leadership by political elites.Sonia was also defensive when asked about the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, which remained in power for a decade until 2014, and the controversies surrounding its tenure.“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” she said, responding to the criticism.Sonia calls Emergency a mistakeThe conversation also turned to the Emergency imposed by her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi, in 1975.She described the decision as a “mistake” and said she believed Indira herself eventually came to feel the same way.“I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her,” the ex-Congress president said.Sonia said the Gandhi family was “split on the decision” to impose the Emergency.According to the newspaper's account, her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, opposed the move and advised his mother to wait for the next election. Her younger son, Sanjay Gandhi, reportedly pushed for a tougher response to the Opposition.At a family dinner, Sanjay is said to have warned Indira that the Opposition would destroy her, telling her, “They must be stopped”. His influence over his mother became a major source of public controversy.Sonia recalled that the decision “inflamed tensions” within the family. Rajiv reportedly tried to confront his mother, but she refused to listen.“Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” it quoted from her book.Recalling the trauma of assassinationsSonia also spoke about the personal trauma of losing her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, who was assassinated in 1991. She struggled to recall how she carried on after his death, with her daughter Priyanka also joining the conversation at her residence.She recalled the assassination of Indira Gandhi in 1984, when she heard what sounded like fireworks before seeing her mother-in-law's body covered in blood and bullet wounds. Indira had been shot by two of her bodyguards.Sonia described trying to revive her as they rushed her to hospital.“There was blood everywhere, and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she remembered.She described the journey to the hospital as “excruciating”. Despite the relatively light traffic, the drive seemed painfully slow. She said she knew Indira might already be dead because she was no longer responding.Sonia also recalled the trauma and depression that followed, saying she lived “like a ghost”. The conversation touched on Rajiv's private expression of grief during that difficult period.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Always found her way to the finish line': Family releases obituary for NYC Marathon runner Rachel Apa who died from rhabdomyolysis
articles.summary: The family of Rachel Apa, the 24-year-old runner who died after collapsing just two miles short of the finish line at the New York City Marathon, has
articles.body: The family of Rachel Apa, the 24-year-old runner who died after collapsing just two miles short of the finish line at the New York City Marathon, has released a moving obituary remembering her as a determined athlete who "always found her way to the finish line".Apa, from Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, collapsed near Mile 24 of the marathon in Central Park on November 1. She was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital but died hours later. Her family said she suffered from rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition involving the breakdown of muscle tissue."With determination, discipline, and a heart fully committed to whatever she pursued, she always found her way to the finish line," her family wrote in the obituary.Recalling her final moments during the race, the family wrote that Apa had completed 24 miles at an incredible pace, with a wide grin on her face."On Sunday, November 1, 2026, after running 24 miles at an incredible pace and with a grin that stretched ear to ear, the only thing strong enough to physically stop her body met Rachel on 85th Street," the obituary said."Her spirit was so powerful and full of vitality that not even her body could contain it," the family added.The obituary described Apa as strong-willed and someone who naturally took charge. Despite being just 24, she had already achieved several milestones and inspired pride among those who knew her."At just 24, Rachel had already accomplished so much and given those who knew her countless reasons to be proud. She moved through the world with purpose, always setting high expectations for herself," her family wrote.Beyond athletics, Apa was passionate about animals, particularly her dogs, whom her family described as her "forever children". She was also a talented baker who had created a cookie recipe so irresistible that her family joked they had to get rid of it for the sake of their health."She created a cookie recipe so perfect it had to be thrown away for the sake of our health," the obituary read.Apa was a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University. She graduated from the university in 2024 and had been pursuing a master's degree in business administration at Charleston Southern University while working.She was running her first New York City Marathon to raise money for Parkinson's disease research in honour of her grandfather, who died of the disease in 2022.In a LinkedIn post before the race, Apa had credited her grandfather with teaching her to remain active, push her limits and embrace challenges."My grandfather was one of my role models growing up. He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges," she had written.Her father, Steve Apa, had earlier said his daughter was in excellent health and had trained for the marathon. He had been exchanging text messages with her throughout the race, but communication stopped when she reached Mile 24.According to her family, doctors told them that she died from rhabdomyolysis, a potentially life-threatening condition in which damaged muscle tissue releases substances into the bloodstream that can cause kidney damage and other complications.New York Road Runners, which organizes the marathon, said a bystander administered CPR after Apa collapsed. Event medical staff also performed CPR and used a defibrillator before paramedics took her to hospital.The New York City medical examiner's office had said it was investigating her death.You use AI every day. articles.title: New Zealand election: No clear winner after tight general election
articles.summary: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.
articles.body:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.

Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.

But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".

The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.

Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.

The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.

Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".

He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."

Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."

Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".

More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.

But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.

They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.

New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know

The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.

It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.

Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."

Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".

"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.

Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.

The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.

Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders

"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.

Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: She entered Columbia a liberal. A fight over English lit turned her conservative
articles.summary: A Columbia University graduate says speech suppression and grading bias in English classes pushed her from liberalism to the conservative movement.
articles.body: The sharp flick of textbook pages, the smell of studied parchment and a litany of knowledge surrounded Liza Libes during her time at Columbia University, an experience she entered as a bright-eyed, liberal freshman, before leaving a conservative with a deep commitment to free speech. "I was very upset with my suppression of speech. You know, I'm a writer. The biggest thing to me is the ability to be able to say what you think, to write what you think. And I wasn't able to write exactly what I thought in my English classrooms," Libes told Fox News Digital. "I would get Cs when I would argue in favor of the patriarchy. And then when I argued that, you know, so-and-so was subverting gender norms, then I would get an A… It was just this kind of gradual accumulation," she continued. OKLAHOMA STUDENT FLUNKED BY TA AFTER TOUTING CHRISTIAN BELIEFS IN GENDER ESSAY, DIRECTS OTHERS TO ‘PUSH BACK’ Libes detailed an experience she had during an English class involving an assignment about Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream," in which her professor said the play centered on "queer desire." Libes, the founder of the Substack "Pens & Poison," disagreed. "I just wrote about the play, I didn't touch on queer desire. She took off a couple points from my exam because I didn't mention queer desire in the class for the midterm. So I thought that was a very bizarre thing for her to do," she said. "There [were] a couple other professors [that] I really disagreed with in terms of the way that they were teaching literature, the way they were kind of creating this Marxist ideology from a lot of literary works and kind of thrusting the Marxist teachings on so many great works of literature," Libes continued. LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT "I felt very stifled as a writer and I think that that was kind of my last straw," Libes added. "I wanted to be in a place where I could just… express my values, express my beliefs in writing and also in conversation… By the time I was a senior, I very much identified with the conservative movement," she continued. Libes received a master's degree in English and comparative literature in 2020, after earning her bachelor's degree in English literature in 2019. When asked about the campus environment beyond the classroom, Libes described an underlying "expectation" to hold "certain viewpoints," saying she knew she was going to be "socially ostracized in some way." FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS Libes grew up in what she called a "post-Soviet household," speaking Russian with her immigrant parents and grandmother. "One of the things that was very big in my household was just this idea of freedom, right, because my parents had come from the Soviet Union, there was a lot of oppression there," she said. "Obviously, we did not like socialism because socialism was one of the ways that a lot of this oppression was perpetrated. And I thought of myself always as a liberal because I stood for freedom. I was against oppression, I was, you know, pro-free speech — those to me were very liberal ideas, those were the ideas that I grew up with in my household," Libes continued. 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS "When I got to Columbia, I very quickly realized that those ideas were no longer part of the left, that the left liked to suppress speech, the left liked to ostracize anyone who didn't hold, you know, certain opinions or beliefs," she added. Libes encourages other young people to stand by what they believe. "Don't be afraid [of] expressing your beliefs and don't let, kind of, peer pressure or other people sway you into believing one thing or another," Libes said. articles.title: Buildings evacuated in Liverpool city centre after car crash causes gas leak
articles.summary: The impact of the crash caused a gas leak and neighbouring buildings have been evacuated as a precaution.
articles.body:
A car has crashed into a restaurant in Liverpool city centre prompting nearby buildings to be evacuations and road closures due to a gas leak.

The incident happened at about 12:30 GMT on North John Street when a Peugeot car hit the window of Tiger Rock Restaurant, Merseyside Police said.

The driver stayed at the scene and there is no indication that this was a deliberate act, the force said.

Three people who had been in the restaurant at the time of the crash were assessed for minor injuries, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

A spokesman said the impact caused a gas leak so a cordon has been put in place by firefighters and the police, with a structural engineer and a gas engineer due to attend.

Neighbouring buildings have been evacuated as a precaution and road closures are in place at the junction of Dale Street and North John Street, and also the junction of North John Street and Lord Street.

Buses have also been temporarily diverted with all Wirral Metro services terminating at Whitechapel, and starting their return journey from Sir Thomas Street.

articles.title: At least five people killed in shooting in Poland’s Krakow
articles.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says police are investigating after ‘tragic shooting’ in second-largest city.
articles.body:
Five people have been killed and others wounded in a shooting near the main ‌‌market square of Krakow in southern Poland.

At around 3pm (14:00GMT) on Saturday, a man who had driven onto the city’s Main Market Square “began firing at random people from his car”, police said on X.

“As a result of the incident, five people were killed and around a dozen others were wounded,” a police spokesman told the AFP news agency.

The gunman was shot by officers and detained, police said. He was transported to hospital after sustaining injuries.

Police officers were also among the wounded.

“According ⁠to information from police officers, the man was wearing military-style attire,” a police spokesperson told reporters.

“During the arrest, ⁠officers used their weapons, but the man returned fire; ⁠as a result, two ⁠police officers are among the injured,” he added.

A “tragic shooting” took place on Saturday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a post on X.

“I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow,” he wrote, adding that “the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack”.

President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, those affected, ‌and ‌their families.

Tom Rose, the US ambassador to Poland, wrote on X: “We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland.”

He said “America stands with Poland at this dark hour” as Poland stands with the citizens of Krakow.

Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and about 250 kilometres (155 miles) south of the capital, Warsaw.

articles.title: 14 bighas and a family feud: How ancestral land dispute erupted into gunfire in Patna, leaving 6 injured
articles.summary: PATNA: A long-standing dispute over 12-14 bighas of ancestral land triggered a violent clash between two groups of the same extended family in Hiranandpur
articles.body: PATNA: A long-standing dispute over 12-14 bighas of ancestral land triggered a violent clash between two groups of the same extended family in Hiranandpur village, under the Didarganj police station area in Patna, on Saturday afternoon. Six people were injured in the incident, while police detained eight people for questioning.The injured included Dwarka Prasad, the brother of Suresh Yadav, and his three sons, who belong to one group. From the opposing group, Ranjeet Yadav and his brother Arun Kumar also sustained injuries. All the injured were taken to NMCH, Patna, for treatment. The nature and severity of their injuries are yet to be confirmed.According to preliminary information, a tractor was being used to plough the disputed field when an argument broke out over ownership of the land. The disagreement soon escalated into a violent confrontation, with both groups accusing each other of assault and firing. One side alleged that Ranjeet took a rifle from his private security guard and opened fire. However, the opposing group accused Suresh and his family members of attacking them.Didarganj SHO Sunil Kumar said eight people had been detained in connection with the incident. "Both groups belong to the same extended family and have been involved in a dispute over 12-14 bighas of ancestral land for a long time. Both sides claim ownership of the property," he said.Fatuha SDPO Awadhesh Kumar said two firearms and 18 live rounds had been seized. The crime scene was secured and the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) was called to collect evidence. Weapons reportedly carried by the security personnel of both groups, which are said to be licensed, were also being examined. Police received information about the incident around 3pm and reached the village by 3.15pm.Meanwhile, Suresh has a criminal history, with around seven to eight cases registered against him at Didarganj and Shastri Nagar police stations. articles.title: Five people killed, multiple injured in Poland market shooting
articles.summary: Authorities in Poland are investigating a shooting that left five people dead and at least a dozen injured in the Main Market Square in Krakow, a cultural center of the historic city, according to officials.
articles.body: Authorities in Poland are investigating a shooting that left five people dead and at least a dozen injured in the Main Market Square in Krakow, a cultural center of the historic city, according to officials. The shooter was shot by police at the scene and taken to the hospital around 3 p.m. local time. The shots were fired from a vehicle moving through the area, Krakow officials said in a series of posts X. An earlier post from the city’s official municipal government account said that investigators were working to determine the scale of the incident. Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the perpetrator was wearing military-style fatigues and he used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also wrote on social media that police were trying to determine the circumstances surrounding the attack. “We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland,” Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. “America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow.” The Main Market Square sits at the heart of Krakow’s medieval Old Town. Laid out in 1257, the sprawling plaza is home to the historic Cloth Hall and St. Mary’s Basilica.

articles.title: Indian-American Priya Sundareshan elected Arizona Senate president as Democrats secure historic state control
articles.summary: Priya Sundareshan has been elected president of the Arizona Senate, making history as Democrats gain control of the state legislature and governor's office for the first time in 60 years.
articles.body: Indian-American politician Priya Sundareshan has been elected president of the Arizona Senate, as Democrats prepare to take control of the state legislature and governor's office for the first time in 60 years, PTI reported.Sundareshan, 42, has served three terms in the state Senate and was the minority leader in the outgoing chamber. Her election comes as Democrats secure control of both legislative chambers and the governor's mansion, marking a significant shift in Arizona's political landscape.Addressing the development, Sundareshan said the party's victory brought a responsibility to deliver changes that voters could see in their everyday lives.“Wherever you live and whoever you voted for, we're here to work for you,” she said.She added that voters had created an opportunity for a historic change in the state and called on Democrats to focus on their responsibilities.“Voters have opened the door to historic change. Our responsibility is to make sure they feel that change in their daily lives. Let's get to work,” Sundareshan said.She also described the election outcome as a rejection of what she called “MAGA extremism” promoted by Republicans in Arizona.Born in Tucson, Arizona, Sundareshan comes from an Indian-American family. Before entering politics, she taught natural resources law at the University of Arizona and worked with the Environmental Defence Fund, advocating sustainable management of natural resources, according to the news agency.She has also been involved in voting rights initiatives, leading voter protection efforts and working on redistricting within the Arizona Democratic Party.Sundareshan graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2006 with a Bachelor of Science degree in chemical engineering. articles.title: Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers killed in armed attack
articles.summary: It happened in a region of the country known to have drug trafficking activity.
articles.body:
A Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers have been killed in an armed attack, according to the country’s authorities.

The attack on Friday targeted Congressman Julio Portillo, who was in the town of Rio Hondo, in the eastern Zacapa department, which is known for drug trafficking activity.

Portillo was initially taken to a hospital with serious injuries. His death was ‌later confirmed by the National Unity of Hope party, or UNE, to which he belonged.

“President Luis Contreras, members of the Board of Directors and lawmakers mourn the tragic passing of Congressman Julio Cesar Portillo Paz, representative of the Zacapa district,” Guatemala’s Congress posted late Friday on X.

President Bernardo Arevalo said the three National Civil Police officers killed in the attack had died in the line of duty and instructed security forces to ⁠cooperate with prosecutors investigating the killings.

Authorities have not disclosed a motive for the attack or identified ⁠who was responsible.

The Lorenzana family cartel, which has links to Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel, controls the drug trade in Zacapa.

Portillo won his seat in 2023 for the opposition party Cabal, but has since switched to the National Unity of Hope party led by former First Lady Sandra Torres.

She is expected to run for president in Guatemala’s elections next year.

The killings come ⁠about three weeks after former anticorruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was shot dead in Guatemala City, a case that ‌heightened concerns about organised crime’s influence and the possible return of politically motivated assassinations.

Authorities have not established ‌a ‌connection between the two attacks.
